fetched_contents.text: How fragmentation and corridors affect wind dynamics and seed dispersal in open habitats Significance Understanding how widespread human-induced global changes are affecting the movement and dispersal of organisms is critical for maintaining species diversity and making sound land management decisions. In contrast with animal-dispersed species, little is known about how wind-dispersed species are affected by conservation strategies such as corridors. We use a combination of mechanistic models and field data to show that habitat corridors alter wind dynamics in a way that promotes seed dispersal and appears to increase plant diversity. Wind direction also interacts with landscape orientation to determine when corridors can provide connectivity. Keywords: diversity, plant community, habitat structure, reserve design, long-distance dispersal Abstract Determining how widespread human-induced changes such as habitat loss, landscape fragmentation, and climate instability affect populations, communities, and ecosystems is one of the most pressing environmental challenges. Critical to this challenge is understanding how these changes are affecting the movement abilities and dispersal trajectories of organisms and what role conservation planning can play in promoting movement among remaining fragments of suitable habitat. Whereas evidence is mounting for how conservation strategies such as corridors impact animal movement, virtually nothing is known for species dispersed by wind, which are often mistakenly assumed to not be limited by dispersal. Here, we combine mechanistic dispersal models, wind measurements, and seed releases in a large-scale experimental landscape to show that habitat corridors affect wind dynamics and seed dispersal by redirecting and bellowing airflow and by increasing the likelihood of seed uplift. Wind direction interacts with landscape orientation to determine when corridors provide connectivity. Our results predict positive impacts of connectivity and patch shape on species richness of wind-dispersed plants, which we empirically illustrate using 12 y of data from our experimental landscapes. We conclude that habitat fragmentation and corridors strongly impact the movement of wind-dispersed species, which has community-level consequences. ---------------------------------------- Habitat loss and fragmentation sever movement pathways, posing major risks to population persistence and community diversity (1). As a result, landscape connectivity––the degree to which landscapes facilitate movement––is receiving growing attention as a means to increase long-distance dispersal (LDD) of individuals and persistence of species under global change (2, 3). In particular, habitat corridors, or linear strips of habitat connecting otherwise isolated habitat patches, have become one of the most commonly applied conservation tools (4, 5). However, corridors (and connectivity more generally) are almost exclusively considered a conservation strategy for animals or animal-dispersed organisms, not for the great diversity of species that are passively transported by wind. Wind is a frequent means of movement for many organisms, including plant seeds, pollen, spores, insects, and pathogens (6–8). The changes in habitat structure (e.g., edge creation) that accompany habitat fragmentation and connectivity may strongly influence the flow of air, particularly the amount of vertical uplifting––a critical factor known to drive LDD of seeds by wind (9–11). Over the past decade, our mechanistic understanding of wind-driven seed dispersal has substantially increased (12, 13) and models have begun to incorporate landscape heterogeneity (11, 14–18). Combining mechanistic insight from dispersal models with dispersal patterns from real landscapes is the next frontier in understanding dispersal in fragmented habitats (12, 19–21). Gaining a mechanistic understanding of how habitat fragmentation and connectivity affect wind dispersal (and dispersal in general), however, has proven challenging: whereas short-distance dispersal events can be empirically quantified, LDD events––the unusually long movements accomplished by only a small fraction of individuals in a population (Materials and Methods and SI Materials and Methods)––are difficult to detect empirically. As a consequence, LDD events are typically predicted using mechanistic models, but these predictions are rarely empirically tested (19). Here, we surmount these challenges by combining predictions for wind dynamics and seed dispersal patterns from an advanced fluid-dynamics model with empirical wind and seed dispersal data from a unique large-scale landscape fragmentation experiment that controls for patch area, shape, and connectivity. This comprehensive approach allows for evaluation of habitat fragmentation and connectivity impacts on both short- and long-distance dispersal of seeds by wind. Our work reveals several revealing mechanisms by which landscape structure impacts the movement of wind-dispersed plants, and demonstrates how landscape effects on wind can have consequences for plant community diversity. We developed and tested our model predictions within a large-scale experimental landscape (∼50 ha) at the Savannah River Site, SC (Fig. 1) comprising 1.375 ha connected and unconnected open-habitat longleaf pine savanna patches surrounded by mature pine plantation. “Connected” patches test for connectivity effects whereas unconnected “rectangular” and “winged” patches test for patch area and shape effects, respectively (Materials and Methods). Longleaf pine savanna supports some of the most diverse plant communities in the world (22, 23) and is typified in part by a large proportion of wind-dispersed plant species (22). At our study site, for example, wind-dispersed species constitute the most common plant dispersal mode. fetched_contents.text: Short seed‐dispersal distances and low seedling recruitment in farmland populations of bird‐dispersed cherry trees - Breitbach - 2012 - Journal of Ecology Introduction Human-modified landscapes dominate most terrestrial ecosystems around the globe (Millennium Ecosystem Assessment (MEA) 2005; Tylianakis et al. 2008). In temperate regions, human land-use intensification has been particularly strong and agricultural landscapes have experienced substantial modifications (Foley et al. 2005; Millennium Ecosystem Assessment (MEA) 2005; UNEP 2007). These processes have created isolated patches of semi-natural habitats within an intensively utilized agricultural matrix, which has important consequences for the dynamics of plant (Cain, Milligan & Strand 2000; García & Chacoff 2007) and animal populations (Howe & Miriti 2004; Tylianakis, Tscharntke & Lewis 2007). Plant populations in intensively used landscapes are usually patchily distributed (Franzén & Nilsson 2010). Many plants depend on animal vectors, often birds, for the movement of their seeds among these habitat patches (Snow & Snow 1988; Levey et al. 2005; Jordano et al. 2011). Birds can act as ‘mobile links’ between plant populations and transport seeds over long distances through unfavourable habitats and can, hence, interconnect isolated plant populations (e.g. Lundberg & Moberg 2003; Breitbach et al. 2010; García, Zamora & Amico 2010). Previous studies have found that flight and thus dispersal distances were longer in structurally simple agricultural landscapes than in forest (Gómez 2003; Lenz et al. 2011). So far, many studies have investigated seed dispersal only in terms of dispersal distance (e.g. Holbrook & Smith 2000; Westcott & Graham 2000; Westcott et al. 2005; Lenz et al. 2011). However, from the plants' perspective, it is not only important how far seeds get dispersed but also where seeds are finally deposited (Schupp, Jordano & Gómez 2010). The ‘Directed Dispersal Hypothesis’ (sensu Howe & Smallwood 1982) predicts that animal vectors can increase the probability that seeds are transferred to sites with suitable conditions for plant recruitment (Wenny 2001), thereby increasing recruitment success (Wenny & Levey 1998). Directed dispersal is particularly important in human-modified landscapes where suitable habitats are patchily distributed (Cain, Milligan & Strand 2000; García & Chacoff 2007) and where many seeds are prone to be dropped into the unsuitable habitat matrix (Schupp 1993; Cain, Milligan & Strand 2000; Nathan 2006; Schurr, Steinitz & Nathan 2008). Consequently, seed deposition in suitable habitats is expected to be lower in landscapes where suitable habitats are patchily distributed, such as farmland, than in homogeneous forests (Dunford & Freemark 2004; Westcott et al. 2005; García, Zamora & Amico 2010). A valuable approach to assess how seed-dispersal services by birds change along a land-use gradient is to combine movement data of animal dispersal vectors, for example, from radio tracking, with their gut retention time of seeds (Westcott et al. 2005; Lenz et al. 2011). Movement data and retention times can be integrated in predictive models of the distribution of seed-dispersal distances provided by animal vectors. However, previous studies using this approach did not incorporate habitat requirements of the studied plant species into their model (Westcott & Graham 2000; Spiegel & Nathan 2007; García, Zamora & Amico 2010; Lenz et al. 2011; Karubian et al. 2012) and thus did not account for seed fate after dispersal which ultimately translates into recruitment success (Schupp, Jordano & Gómez 2010). Hence, there is a lack of studies that have linked predicted patterns of seed deposition with estimates of plant recruitment, such as seedling recruitment and survival (but see McConkey & Brockelman 2011). We therefore know little about how seeds are distributed in human-modified landscapes and how patterns of seed deposition translate into plant recruitment success. In this study, we integrate movement data and seed regurgitation times of the Common Blackbird (Turdus merula L.) in a simulation model to predict seed-dispersal distances and locations of seeds of wild cherry trees (Prunus avium L.) in forest and farmland habitats in a human-modified landscape. The wild cherry is one of the most widespread bird-dispersed tree species in Central Europe; blackbirds are the most important seed dispersers of many woody species in this region (Snow & Snow 1988; Breitbach et al. 2010). We recorded in a previous study that birds remove wild cherry seeds at similarly high frequencies in forest and farmland habitats (Breitbach et al. 2010). However, we do not know how seed-dispersal distances and locations change along the forest-farmland gradient. We therefore analysed movement behaviour of blackbirds in forest and farmland and combined these data with regurgitation times of wild cherry seeds. Our main objectives were to model distributions of seed-dispersal distances of wild cherries in forest and farmland habitats and to predict probabilities of seed deposition in habitats suitable for seedling recruitment. We related the findings of the model to the observed patterns of seedling recruitment of wild cherries in forest and farmland. We tested the following hypotheses: (i) seed-dispersal distances are longer in farmland than in forest because we expected longer flight distances of blackbirds in farmland than in forest. (ii) The probability of seed deposition in suitable habitat is higher in forest than in farmland where suitable habitats are more patchily distributed. To test whether these potential differences in seed dispersal were related to recruitment success, we compared seedling recruitment of wild cherries between forest and farmland habitats. The overlooked role of unpaved roads in endozoochorous seed dispersal - Suárez‐Esteban - 2013 - Journal of Applied Ecology Introduction Land-use change is one of the main components of global change (Foley et al. 2005) and one of the most important drivers of biodiversity loss (Vitousek et al. 1997). This involves the transformation of natural or semi-natural habitats into croplands, pastures and urban land (Lambin & Geist 2006). Such modifications are almost invariably associated with linear developments such as roads, highways, tracks, railways and firebreaks. These structures have reached an extremely high density world-wide (Forman 1998). Some linear developments such as paved roads and highways are usually wide, noisy (due to high traffic levels) and even fenced. Because their effects extent beyond their boundaries, habitat loss, fragmentation and limited animal and plant dispersal are among their known effects (Forman & Alexander 1998; Trombulak & Frissell 2000). However, other types of linear developments such as dirt tracks, logging roads and firebreaks, hereafter described as ‘Soft’ Linear Developments (SLD), represent much lighter landscape alterations, having probably subtle and unknown ecological effects. Given that SLD represent a form of clearing, the lack of vegetation means that they can facilitate the movement of terrestrial animals (Kuefler et al. 2010), acting as corridors (Haddad et al. 2003; Haddad & Tewksbury 2005). Moreover, some studies suggested that experimental linear clearings immerse in a forest matrix may enhance ecosystem services such as seed dispersal (Tewksbury et al. 2002; Levey et al. 2005), which is essential for plant populations (Levin et al. 2003), and boosts biodiversity conservation (Damschen et al. 2006; Ozinga et al. 2009). Could other similar linear clearings such as SLD also promote seed dispersal? Although linear developments are known to assist the spread of some alien species (Gelbard & Belnap 2003; Christen & Matlack 2006), very little is known about their potential effects on native populations (but see Tikka, Högmander & Koski 2001; Karim & Mallik 2008). This lack of knowledge is especially surprising in the case of plants, since their mobility is limited and relies on dispersal vectors that are likely to interact with prominent landscape elements (Damschen et al. 2008) such as linear developments. Indeed, whereas some vertebrates avoid them (Forman & Alexander 1998; James & Stuart-Smith 2000), many seed-dispersing mammals all over the world, such as the red fox Vulpes vulpes L. (Rost, Pons & Bas 2012), the coyote Canis latrans Say (Fedriani & Kohn 2001), the martens Martes spp (López-Bao & González-Varo 2011) and the European rabbit Oryctolagus cuniculus L. (Authors unpublished data), seem to positively select SLD verges for defecation. Frugivorous mammals ingest and disperse viable seeds of a huge variety of both native and exotic fleshy-fruit plant species world-wide (Myers, Vellend & Gardescu 2004; Stoner et al. 2007; Matias et al. 2010). Many of these terrestrial dispersers may deposit viable seeds along SLD verges (see references above), presumably with consequences for the dynamic and the spatial and genetic structures of plant populations (Howe & Miriti 2000; Nathan & Muller-Landau 2000; Levin et al. 2003). Furthermore, mammals are highly mobile and disperse seeds through long distances (Jordano et al. 2007). Such long-distance seed dispersal events usually imply plant fitness advantages (Levin et al. 2003; Nathan 2006). Despite their potential for fragmenting the landscape for some dispersers, SLD may also connect isolated plant populations by enhancing long-distance seed dispersal by other species. Dispersed seeds often lead to established plants (Howe & Miriti 2000); therefore, SLD verges could be reforested by some mammal-dispersed plants (Karim & Mallik 2008). By promoting plant dispersion, SLD would be acting as corridors connecting the landscape at large. Even though these potential effects are likely to occur and could have important ecological and applied consequences, these intriguing possibilities had not been considered to date. In this study, we examine whether SLD influence mammal-generated seed rains (i.e. spatial distribution of dispersed seeds). Although from a plant ‘perspective’ the absolute number of seeds effectively dispersed is the important factor, dissecting seed dispersal qualitative and quantitative components is important to understand such complex processes (Schupp, Jordano & Gómez 2010). In the case of endozoochorous plants (plants dispersed through ingestion by animal), the abundance and the spatial distribution of dispersed seeds are determined by the abundance and distribution of faeces containing viable seeds. This in turn is a function of (i) the spatial pattern of defecation of frugivores, (ii) their fruit consumption (i.e. proportion of faeces with fruit remains) and (iii) whether they damage the seeds they ingest. To assess in detail whether such mammal-generated seed rain components are influenced by SLD, we chose several patches of Mediterranean scrubland in south-western Spain characterized by a diverse community of fleshy-fruit shrubs and frugivorous mammals, as well as a vast SLD system. Previous studies and observations suggest that carnivores and rabbits often defecate along SLD verges (Fedriani, Palomares & Delibes 1999), while ungulates generally avoid these structures (James & Stuart-Smith 2000). Furthermore, carnivores are recognized as legitimate seed dispersers (Herrera 1989; López-Bao & González-Varo 2011), whereas ungulates and rabbits often act as seed predators rather than dispersers (Fedriani & Delibes 2009b; Perea et al. 2012). Consequently, the potential role of SLD as seed attractors was expected to depend on the species-specific defecation places and dispersal effectiveness (sensu Schupp, Jordano & Gómez 2010) of dispersal vectors. Ecological mechanisms that limit corridor effectiveness for seed dispersal

Corridors can fail to enhance seed dispersal because they often do not address the broader ecological processes that structure dispersal. The evidence shows that habitat fragmentation and corridors can alter wind dynamics in a way that promotes seed dispersal in some cases, but the same study also notes that corridors are almost exclusively considered for animal or animal-dispersed organisms rather than wind-dispersed species, and that wind-dispersed species are often mistakenly assumed to be unconstrained by dispersal [N1-F1]. This mismatch is important: corridors may be physically present, but if they do not align with the movement mechanisms of the species in question, they can still fail to support dispersal.

One key ecological process is that corridors can create new barriers rather than remove them. The same source states that habitat loss and fragmentation sever movement pathways, and corridors are one of the most commonly applied conservation tools for connectivity [N1-F1]. But the study’s main conclusion is that corridors strongly impact the movement of wind-dispersed species, which has community-level consequences. That means corridors are not neutral; they change airflow and seed dynamics, which can either help or hinder dispersal depending on the species and the corridor design [N1-F1]. The evidence also notes that wind direction interacts with landscape orientation to determine when corridors provide connectivity [N1-F1]. This implies that corridors may support dispersal in some orientations and not in others, so their utility depends on alignment with the prevailing wind regime and landscape structure.

Corridor width, connectivity, and patch arrangement matter because corridors are linear structures whose effectiveness depends on how they connect habitat patches. The N1 evidence emphasizes that corridors alter wind dynamics and seed dispersal by redirecting and bellowing airflow and by increasing the likelihood of seed uplift [N1-F1]. That suggests that wider or more continuous corridors may be more effective at redirecting airflow and promoting long-distance seed movement. At the same time, the study notes that corridors can only provide connectivity when wind direction and landscape orientation are favorable [N1-F1]. So corridor effectiveness is not just a matter of presence; it depends on spatial arrangement, corridor shape, and the interaction between corridor design and wind patterns.

For patch arrangement, the evidence points to the importance of connectivity versus isolation. The N1 source discusses connected patches versus unconnected rectangular and winged patches, and concludes that connectivity and patch shape have positive impacts on species richness of wind-dispersed plants [N1-F1]. In other words, corridors are only useful if they connect otherwise isolated patches and are arranged in a way that enhances connectivity. The same source also highlights that long-distance dispersal events are difficult to detect empirically, but that corridors can affect short- and long-distance dispersal patterns [N1-F1]. This matters because many seed dispersal studies focus on dispersal distance, but corridor effectiveness can depend on whether the corridor helps seeds reach suitable habitats rather than just moving them longer distances [N1-F1].

Species traits determine corridor effectiveness because some species are more sensitive to corridor design and matrix quality. The N3 evidence is especially strong on this point. It states that in fragmented landscapes, habitat patches are surrounded by an unsuitable matrix, and the matrix often acts as a strong barrier to dispersal [N3-R3]. That means corridors may not help if the surrounding matrix is hostile. The same source also reports that seedling recruitment was not associated with seed dispersal rates, even for actively dispersed seeds [N3-R1]. That suggests that the ultimate success of a corridor depends on seed fate after dispersal, not just the movement of seeds themselves.

Animal-mediated dispersal has different constraints than wind-mediated dispersal. The N3 evidence shows that many plants depend on animal vectors for seed dispersal, and that seed deposition in suitable habitats is expected to be lower in landscapes where suitable habitats are patchily distributed [N3-F2]. It also notes that the directed dispersal hypothesis predicts that animal vectors can increase the probability that seeds are transferred to sites with suitable conditions for plant recruitment [N3-F2]. This is a critical point: corridors can fail if they do not provide suitable deposition sites, even if they increase seed movement. In contrast, wind-dispersed species are affected by corridor-mediated changes in wind dynamics and uplift [N1-F1], so corridors may support or hinder them depending on wind direction, corridor shape, and landscape orientation [N1-F1].

Species with short dispersal ranges or high matrix sensitivity are especially vulnerable. The N3 evidence emphasizes that seed dispersal distances can be short, and low seedling recruitment can result even when seeds are dispersed [N3-R2]. It also notes that suitable habitats are patchily distributed in human-modified landscapes, so seeds are prone to being dropped into the unsuitable matrix [N3-F2]. This means corridors may not help species that rely on long-distance movement or that cannot tolerate the matrix surrounding the corridor. The same source also states that bird-dispersed cherry trees in farmland showed short seed-dispersal distances and low seedling recruitment [N3-F2]. That illustrates why corridors may fail for species whose dispersal is limited by matrix quality, defecation behavior, or the spatial mismatch between dispersal vectors and suitable habitats [N3-F2].

Overall, the ecological processes that prevent corridors from supporting dispersal include fragmentation-induced movement barriers, mismatch between corridor design and dispersal mechanisms, and the dominance of the surrounding matrix over corridor effectiveness [N1-F1][N3-R3]. Corridor width, connectivity, and patch arrangement matter because corridors alter airflow and seed dynamics, and their utility depends on wind direction, landscape orientation, and whether they connect isolated patches [N1-F1]. Species traits that make corridors less effective include reliance on animal dispersal with poor seed deposition outcomes, short dispersal ranges, and high sensitivity to the matrix surrounding the corridor [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-F2].

Agricultural and landscape context that reduces corridor utility

Farmland fragmentation and matrix quality are central to why corridors may be ineffective. The evidence states that fragmented landscapes create isolated patches surrounded by an unsuitable matrix, and the matrix often acts as a strong barrier to dispersal [N3-R3]. This is especially relevant in farmland environments, where the matrix is usually intensively used agriculture rather than suitable habitat. The same source also notes that many plants depend on animal vectors for seed dispersal, and that seed deposition in suitable habitats is expected to be lower in landscapes where suitable habitats are patchily distributed [N3-F2]. So, corridors may not help if the surrounding matrix is hostile or if the corridor does not provide suitable deposition sites.

Edge effects, fire, and disturbance regimes are important because they shape the corridor environment and can undermine its function. While the provided evidence does not directly cite fire or disturbance regimes in the agricultural context, it does emphasize that fragmented landscapes create edge effects and alter habitat structure [N1-F1][N3-F2]. The wind-dispersed species study explains that habitat fragmentation and corridors alter wind dynamics, and that these changes influence airflow and seed uplift [N1-F1]. Edge effects are therefore relevant because corridors often form new edges that change wind patterns, microclimate, and seed movement trajectories. In farmland, where disturbance is frequent and habitat patches are isolated, corridors may be exposed to repeated disturbance that disrupts dispersal or seed survival [N3-R3].

The role of corridor design relative to species’ movement preferences is also key. The evidence suggests that corridors may not align with species’ movement preferences because some species are wind-dispersed and rely on airflow patterns, while others are animal-dispersed and depend on vectors that may avoid corridors or deposit seeds elsewhere [N1-F1][N3-F2]. The wind-dispersed study emphasizes that corridors can promote seed dispersal if wind direction and landscape orientation are favorable, but this is not always the case [N1-F1]. For animal-dispersed species, corridors may fail if the surrounding matrix is unsuitable, because suitable habitats are patchily distributed and seeds are often dropped into the matrix [N3-F2]. This mismatch between corridor structure and species behavior is one reason corridors can fail in farmland: they may increase movement opportunities but not improve deposition success.

Fragmentation and matrix quality reduce corridor utility by severing movement pathways and creating barriers. The evidence shows that habitat loss and fragmentation sever movement pathways, and corridors are one of the most commonly applied conservation tools for connectivity [N1-F1]. But the same study notes that corridors strongly impact wind-dispersed species, with community-level consequences [N1-F1]. This means corridors are not simply passive connectors; they change the landscape in ways that can either help or hinder dispersal. In farmland, where the matrix is often agricultural land that is not suitable for many species, corridors may not provide meaningful connectivity because the surrounding matrix is not conducive to dispersal [N3-R3].

The evidence also implies that corridor utility depends on the broader landscape structure. The wind-dispersed study discusses connected patches versus unconnected patches and concludes that connectivity and patch shape have positive impacts on species richness of wind-dispersed plants [N1-F1]. That suggests that corridors are only effective if they connect isolated patches and are arranged to enhance connectivity. In agricultural landscapes, where habitat patches are often small and surrounded by a hostile matrix, corridors may be ineffective unless they are part of a larger network that includes stepping stones, refuges, or other dispersal infrastructure [N1-F1]. The evidence does not explicitly mention stepping stones in the provided material, but it does support the general principle that corridor design must align with species’ movement preferences and matrix quality [N3-R3][N3-F2].

In short, farmland fragmentation and matrix quality reduce corridor utility by creating barriers, patchily distributed suitable habitats, and an unsuitable surrounding matrix [N3-R3][N3-F2]. Edge effects and disturbance regimes are relevant because they alter corridor structure and seed movement dynamics [N1-F1]. Corridors may not align with species’ movement preferences because wind-dispersed species depend on airflow patterns and animal-dispersed species depend on vectors that may avoid corridors or deposit seeds in unsuitable habitats [N1-F1][N3-F2]. Overall, corridor utility in farmland is constrained by the quality of the surrounding matrix, the spatial arrangement of patches, and the mismatch between corridor design and species-specific movement requirements [N1-F1][N3-R3][N3-F2].

Management and design failures that undermine corridor success

Common corridor design flaws include isolation and linear configuration. The evidence shows that corridors are often treated as linear strips connecting otherwise isolated habitat patches, but this design may be inadequate when the surrounding matrix is unsuitable or when species require more complex connectivity [N3-R3][N1-F1]. The wind-dispersed study emphasizes that corridors alter wind dynamics and seed dispersal, but that corridors can only provide connectivity when wind direction and landscape orientation are favorable [N1-F1]. This suggests that linear corridors may not be sufficient on their own; their effectiveness depends on spatial arrangement, orientation, and the prevailing environmental conditions. The same source also discusses connected versus unconnected patches and patch shape, implying that isolated corridors may not support dispersal if they do not connect effectively to larger habitat networks [N1-F1].

Lack of dispersal infrastructure such as stepping stones or refuges can reduce corridor effectiveness. While the provided evidence does not explicitly cite “stepping stones” as a term, it does support the broader principle that corridors need to connect isolated patches and that connectivity and patch shape matter [N1-F1][N3-R3]. The wind-dispersed study concludes that connectivity and patch shape have positive impacts on species richness of wind-dispersed plants [N1-F1]. That implies that corridors should be part of a larger network rather than standalone linear features. The evidence also notes that seedling recruitment was not associated with seed dispersal rates, even for actively dispersed seeds [N3-R1]. This suggests that corridors may fail if they do not provide suitable deposition sites, which is a form of missing dispersal infrastructure. In farmland, where the matrix is often hostile and suitable habitats are patchily distributed, corridors may be ineffective unless they are embedded in a landscape that includes refuges or other habitat elements that support recruitment [N3-R3][N3-F2].

Maintenance and land-use change can undermine corridors over time. The evidence highlights that habitat fragmentation and corridors strongly impact wind-dispersed species, and that these changes have community-level consequences [N1-F1]. It also notes that long-distance dispersal events are difficult to detect empirically, but that corridors can affect both short- and long-distance dispersal patterns [N1-F1]. This means corridors are not static: their effectiveness can degrade as land use changes, as corridors are altered by human activity, or as the surrounding matrix becomes more hostile [N1-F1][N3-R3]. The human-mediated dispersal evidence adds that humans fundamentally affect dispersal, directly by transporting individuals and indirectly by altering landscapes and natural vectors [N5-F4]. This is especially relevant because corridors may be undermined by ongoing land-use change, such as conversion of natural areas to agriculture, road construction, or other development activities that reduce corridor quality or connectivity [N5-F4].

The evidence also shows that corridors may be affected by the broader policy and implementation context. The human barriers evidence notes that linear developments such as unpaved roads can act as corridors for seed dispersal, but also that some linear developments are wide, noisy, and even fenced, which can limit animal and plant dispersal [N5-F4]. This illustrates that corridor success depends not just on design, but on ongoing management and land-use stability. If corridors are not maintained, or if land use changes around them, their function can be lost [N5-F4]. The evidence further suggests that human-mediated dispersal can “rewire” spatial networks, meaning that corridors may be more or less effective depending on whether human activity enhances or disrupts dispersal pathways [N5-F4].

In summary, common corridor design flaws are isolation and linear configuration, which may not provide sufficient connectivity unless aligned with wind direction, landscape orientation, and species-specific movement preferences [N1-F1]. Lack of dispersal infrastructure such as stepping stones or refuges can reduce corridor effectiveness because corridors need to connect isolated patches and support suitable deposition sites [N1-F1][N3-R1]. Maintenance and land-use change undermine corridors over time because corridors are sensitive to ongoing human activity, matrix changes, and the broader landscape context [N1-F1][N5-F4]. Overall, corridors are vulnerable to failure when design, management, and land-use dynamics do not support long-term connectivity and dispersal success [N1-F1][N5-F4].

Species-specific and functional dispersal limitations that make corridors less effective

Animal-mediated and wind-mediated dispersal respond differently to corridors because they depend on different mechanisms and environmental constraints. The evidence shows that wind-dispersed species are affected by corridor-mediated changes in wind dynamics and uplift, whereas animal-dispersed species are influenced by vector behavior, seed deposition, and matrix quality [N1-F1][N3-F2]. For wind-dispersed species, corridors can promote seed dispersal when wind direction and landscape orientation are favorable, but they can also create barriers if airflow is redirected away from suitable habitats [N1-F1]. For animal-dispersed species, corridors may fail if the surrounding matrix is unsuitable, because suitable habitats are patchily distributed and seeds are often dropped into the matrix [N3-F2]. This means that corridors may help one dispersal mode but not another, and their effectiveness depends on whether they improve movement or improve deposition.

Seed size, dispersal mode, and life history traits are important because they determine how much corridors can influence dispersal. The evidence emphasizes that many plants depend on animal vectors for seed dispersal, and that directed dispersal can increase the probability that seeds are transferred to suitable sites [N3-F2]. It also states that short seed-dispersal distances and low seedling recruitment are common in farmland populations of bird-dispersed cherry trees [N3-R2]. These findings suggest that species with small seeds may have different corridor needs than species with large seeds or different dispersal modes. The wind-dispersed study further shows that wind-dispersed species are often mistakenly assumed to be unconstrained by dispersal, but corridor-mediated changes in airflow can strongly affect movement [N1-F1]. So corridor effectiveness depends not only on seed size but also on whether the species is wind-dispersed, animal-dispersed, or has a dispersal mode that depends on rare long-distance events [N1-F1][N3-F2].

Life history traits matter because they shape corridor requirements. The evidence notes that seedling recruitment was not associated with seed dispersal rates, even for actively dispersed seeds [N3-R1]. That suggests that corridor success depends on post-dispersal survival, germination, and recruitment rather than just movement distance [N3-R1]. It also states that seed deposition in suitable habitats is expected to be lower in landscapes where suitable habitats are patchily distributed [N3-F2]. This implies that species with life histories that depend on deposition in suitable habitats may benefit more from corridors that provide connectivity, while species with life histories that tolerate or require unsuitable habitats may not. The same source also reports that bird-dispersed cherry trees in farmland had short seed-dispersal distances and low seedling recruitment [N3-F2]. This illustrates how life history traits—such as dispersal distance, recruitment success, and reliance on deposition—can make corridors less effective.

Corridors can fail for species with short dispersal ranges or high matrix sensitivity because those species are less likely to overcome the surrounding matrix. The evidence shows that fragmented landscapes often create an unsuitable matrix, and that matrix quality can act as a strong barrier to dispersal [N3-R3]. For species with short dispersal ranges, corridors may not provide enough movement to connect isolated patches. For species with high matrix sensitivity, corridors may not help because the surrounding matrix is hostile and seeds are likely to be deposited in unsuitable habitats [N3-R3][N3-F2]. The wind-dispersed study further indicates that corridors can affect both short- and long-distance dispersal patterns, but long-distance dispersal is difficult to detect empirically [N1-F1]. This means that corridors may help some species only if they enable rare long-distance events, whereas corridors may not help species that rely on frequent short-distance dispersal [N1-F1].

Overall, animal-mediated and wind-mediated dispersal respond differently to corridors because one depends on vector behavior and deposition, while the other depends on airflow and uplift [N1-F1][N3-F2]. Seed size, dispersal mode, and life history traits matter because they determine whether corridors improve movement, deposition, or recruitment [N3-R1][N3-F2]. Corridors can fail for species with short dispersal ranges or high matrix sensitivity because those species may not overcome fragmentation barriers or may be deposited in unsuitable habitats [N3-R3][N3-F2]. In other words, corridors are only effective when they align with the species’ dispersal mode, life history, and sensitivity to the surrounding matrix [N1-F1][N3-F2].
